summary: Hanns Oertel worked in Indology and linguistics. He completed his doctoral degree at Yale under William Dwight Whitney (~1888–1890). He held posts at Yale (1891–1917), Harvard (1903–1904), Basel (1920), Marburg (~1922–1925), and Munich (1925–1935).
Hannu Riikonen studied at the University of Helsinki (~1967–1976). He later served as a professor at the University of Helsinki (~1997–2013).

Hans Hartog was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Tübingen, Kirchliche Hochschule Bethel, Munich, and Marburg, earning his PhD (~1937–1939) under Friedrich Heiler, Johannes Nobel, and Leo Weisgerber. He was also taught by Hanns Oertel and Walther Wüst.
Hans Henrich Hock, active in linguistics and Indology, studied at Yale University (~1965–1971). He served as a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (~1967–2013).

Hans T. Bakker is an Indologist and religious studies scholar who studied under Jacob Ensink (~1972–1982). He held posts at Utrecht University (~1976–1982), the University of Groningen (1990–1995), and the British Museum (~2013).
Hans-Werner Köhler, a scholar in Indology, completed his doctoral studies under Ernst Waldschmidt (until 1948) and was taught by Eduard Hermann.

Hanung Kim, working in Tibetology and history/archaeology, studied at Columbia University (~2010–2012) and earned a PhD at Harvard University (~2012–2018) under doctoral supervisor Leonard van der Kuijp.

Hara Prasad Sastri was an Indologist and Buddhist studies scholar. He held posts as Joint Philological Secretary at the Asiatic Society (~1885–1920) and Principal at Sanskrit College and University (~1900–1908).

Harald Hauptmann worked in history, archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Heidelberg University (~1958–1964) and held posts there (~1980–2001), at the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities (~1989–2018), and at DAI Istanbul (~1994–2001).

Haraprasad Shastri studied at Presidency University, Kolkata, and Sanskrit College and University (~1871–1877). Working in Indology, archaeology, and Buddhist studies, he held posts at Hare School (~1878–1883), Presidency University (~1895–1908), Sanskrit College (~1900–1908), and Dhaka (~1921–1924).

Hari Damodar Velankar was an Indologist who studied under H. M. Bhadkamkar (~1916–1920). He held posts at Wilson College, Mumbai (~1920–1953) and served as Joint Director at Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan (~1953–1963).

Hari Shankar Prasad is a scholar of philosophy, Buddhist studies, and Indology. He studied at Banaras Hindu University under Ramakant Tripathi (1976) and completed his doctoral studies under Jan Willem de Jong (1979–1982).

Haridas Bhattacharyya was a scholar of philosophy and Indology who studied at Scottish Church College (~1908–1912) and the University of Calcutta (~1912–1914). He held posts at Calcutta (~1917–1921), Dhaka (~1921–1947), and Banaras Hindu University.

Harivallabh Bhayani specialized in Indology and linguistics, studying at Samaldas Arts College (~1935–1939) and Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan (~1945–1951). He held posts at Gujarat University (~1965–1975) and served as Director of the L.D. Institute of Indology (~1975).
Harjot Oberoi, a scholar of religious studies and history/archaeology, studied at the Australian National University (~1980–1987) and held a post at the University of British Columbia (~1987).

Harold Conklin, working in linguistics and other fields, studied at the University of California, Berkeley (~1946–1950) and Yale University (~1950–1955). He held a post at Columbia University (~1954–1962).
Harold G. Coward is a scholar of Indology, religious studies, and philosophy. He held posts as a professor at the University of Calgary (~1973–1994) and at the University of Victoria (~1994).
Harold Scheub studied at the University of Michigan (~1954–1960) and the University of Wisconsin-Madison (~1965–1969). He subsequently held a post at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (~1970–2013).
Harold Stewart was a scholar of Buddhist studies who studied at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music and the University of Sydney.

Harold Walter Bailey specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Indology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Western Australia (~1921–1927) and served as a professor at the University of Cambridge (1938–1967).
